item_name: MUR Motorsports (Melbourne University Racing, University of Melbourne)
competition_series: FSAE Australasia (FSAE-A); no evidence found of MUR competing in FSG (Germany), FS UK, or other regional driverless-specific series.
summary: MUR Motorsports began a dedicated driverless sub-program in 2019, alongside its standard electric (EV) car program, explicitly described on the team's own site as 'the start of the development of our EV autonomous FSAE car.' A capstone/junior-project team spent 2019-2021 developing perception (LiDAR clustering, stereo vision, object detection), EKF-SLAM localization, and vehicle-state-estimation (GPS/IMU) subsystems, documented in detail on a dedicated public engineering blog - but validated only in simulation (a forked fssim/Gazebo stack) and on bench rigs, never on a physical FSAE car. In July 2021 the team announced a plan to convert its 2021 competition EV (MUR2021E) into a 2022 driverless mule (MUR2022D) after '18 months of design and simulation.' That conversion did not materialize: MUR's own retrospective states that in 2022 the team 'started afresh focusing solely on building an EV car,' and the base EV vehicle itself failed to pass technical scrutineering or complete a single dynamic event for five straight seasons (2019-2023), only recovering a runnable car in 2024 - as a conventional EV, not a driverless entry. No evidence of any on-vehicle autonomous run, static or dynamic driverless test, or driverless-class competition entry was found at any point. This case is best read as a resourced but ultimately unsuccessful fast-ramp attempt: ambition and real subsystem R&D never converted into a physical driverless run, apparently because the program was run as a side project that lost priority the moment the core EV vehicle needed rescuing.
evidence_quality: moderate to weak - the base EV competition record (technical inspection pass/fail, dynamic events run) is well documented on MUR's own official 'Recent Results' page and is treated as strong evidence. The driverless-specific narrative relies on a team-member engineering blog (active only Mar 2020-Jul 2021, archived via Wayback Machine since the live site now 404s) plus one newsletter and one PCBWay sponsor page; there is no first-hand account, video, or press coverage confirming a physical driverless test ever occurred, so the conclusion that the program never reached an on-vehicle run is an inference from absence of evidence plus explicit 'started afresh' language, not a direct negative confirmation.
dv_program_start: 2019 (H2, best estimate) - MUR's official Recent Results page states '2019 and onwards saw the development of the EV car as well as the start of the development of our EV autonomous FSAE car.' Corroborated by a July 2021 team post citing '18 months of design and simulation' behind the autonomous team, which counts back to roughly early-to-mid 2020, and by the team blog's first post (Mar 2020) already describing an existing two-subsystem driverless team structure.
first_autonomous_run_date: [uncertain] Not found / likely never achieved. No source describes an autonomous run on a physical vehicle at any point 2019-2026.
first_dv_competition: [uncertain] None found. MUR's official results history (2012-2024) lists only Combustion and Electric class results; no driverless/autonomous class entry appears in any year.
months_concept_to_first_autonomous_run: [uncertain] Not applicable - no autonomous run achieved as of 2026 (7+ years after program start), best treated as 'not reached' rather than a numeric duration.
months_concept_to_first_competition: [uncertain] Not applicable - no driverless-class competition entry was ever made.

As of 2026, MUR's own public materials still list 'autonomous (in development)' as a vehicle class, but with no documented progress since the July 2021 post

ramp_phases: Subsystem-only phase (2019-2021, ~2 years): perception, SLAM, and vehicle-state-estimation subsystems developed and demonstrated only in simulation (fssim/Gazebo), on bench rigs (GoPro stereo pair, Piksi GPS/IMU), and even in a commercial racing game (Assetto Corsa, for driver training) - never integrated onto a physical car. Dormant/abandoned phase (2022-2026, ongoing): no documented driverless activity of any kind; team resources visibly redirected to recovering basic EV vehicle functionality.
what_slipped: The July 2021 plan to convert the 2021 competition EV into a 2022 driverless mule (MUR2021E -> MUR2022D) did not materialize - MUR's own later language ('started afresh focusing solely on building an EV car' in 2022) indicates the driverless line item was dropped rather than completed. Separately and more fundamentally, the base EV vehicle program itself failed to pass technical scrutineering or run any dynamic event for 5 of 6 seasons from 2019-2024 (2019: combustion engine failure; 2020-2021: COVID cancellations; 2022: electrical issues; 2023: safety shutdown circuit problems), meaning the prerequisite 'reliable running EV' that the driverless conversion depended on was itself unstable for most of the relevant period. No autonomous run, static test, or dynamic test on a physical vehicle was ever documented.
platform_prerequisites: MUR explicitly planned to require a working EV first - the intended driverless mule was to be a converted prior-year competition car (MUR2021E -> MUR2022D), not a purpose-built driverless platform or a borrowed/spec vehicle (unlike, for example, the shared 'ADS-DV' platform some UK teams use). This EV-first dependency is the most plausible reason the program stalled: when the base EV program itself could not reliably pass scrutineering (2022-2023), the driverless conversion had no stable vehicle to attach to.
ebs_design: N/A - the program never reached vehicle integration, so no EBS was ever built or documented.

compute_platform: [uncertain] Not documented; no onboard compute hardware (Jetson, mini-PC, etc.) was named in any source. Development referenced ROS running on standard development machines for simulation only.
sensor_suite: Bench/simulation-stage components only, never confirmed installed on a competition vehicle: Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR (used for cone-detection/classification simulation and mounting studies per an Aug 2020 blog post), a pair of GoPro Hero 5 Session cameras (early stereo-vision bench rig), Swift Navigation Piksi Multi GPS/IMU receiver kit (Vehicle State Estimation), and later references to Basler cameras and LiDAR in a July 2021 summary of the 'autonomous perception' sub-team.
shutdown_circuit_implementation: N/A for driverless specifically. Note: the base (non-driverless) EV's own low-voltage/safety shutdown circuit was itself a documented point of failure - the 2023 season's dynamic-event absence was explicitly attributed to 'safety shutdown circuit problems.'
custom_pcbs: [uncertain] Not documented for the driverless system specifically; the base EV team references custom PCB work generally, but nothing tied to the driverless program.
software_stack: ROS1 (per the fssim repository documentation, developed/tested on Ubuntu 16.04 with ROS Melodic), C++/Python subsystem repos on GitHub (org: MURDriverless), including mur_common (shared message definitions), HuskyControl (control-algorithm testing on a Clearpath Husky ground robot, apparently used as a physical proxy before car integration), and slowlap_control.
ros_version: ROS1 (Melodic), per the MURDriverless/fssim repository's stated development environment.
perception_approach: LiDAR point-cloud clustering and cylindrical volume reconstruction for cone detection (Ouster OS1-64), developed and demonstrated in simulation and on recorded bench data; a parallel stereo-vision pipeline (GoPro Hero5 bench rig, later reportedly Basler cameras) for redundancy/backup; object-detection experiments are referenced in blog post titles but the specific model/architecture is not detailed in available excerpts.
slam_localization_approach: EKF-SLAM (extended Kalman filter landmark SLAM), explicitly validated in Gazebo simulation and against recorded bench data (per an Aug 2020 'EKFSLAM performance' blog post); a separate Vehicle State Estimation (VSE) subsystem used the Piksi Multi RTK GPS + IMU for odometry/pose, with a documented pivot to a 'COVID-19 GPS/IMU alternative' when the primary hardware became inaccessible during lockdown.
planning_approach: [uncertain] Not documented - the program never reached the planning/control integration stage on a physical vehicle. A dedicated 'Control and path planning' sub-team existed per a March 2020 post, but no specific path-generation method is documented.
control_approach: [uncertain] Not documented with a specific algorithm (e.g., pure pursuit, Stanley, MPC); only the existence of a 'Control and path planning' sub-team is confirmed. The MURDriverless/slowlap_control and HuskyControl repositories suggest control-algorithm work existed, likely tested on a non-FS platform (Husky ground robot), but details are not available.
simulation_tooling: fssim (Formula Student Simulator), a ROS1/Gazebo-based simulator forked from AMZ-Racing's fssim, used to validate perception and SLAM subsystems. The team also, notably, embedded their MUR19E car model into the commercial racing game Assetto Corsa to help drivers learn the competition track - a creative but non-standard simulation use, separate from the driverless-specific fssim work.
ci_cd_testing: [uncertain] A 'continuous integration server' is listed as a 2020 junior-project scope item in the May 2020 team newsletter, but no detail on implementation or coverage was found.
open_source_repos: github.com/MURDriverless (organization) - includes fssim (simulator fork), HuskyControl, slowlap_control, mur_common, and murdriverless.github.io (blog source). Useful as a partial historical reference and as an example of subsystem-level FS driverless code, but the organization and its blog appear inactive since mid-2021 with no further public updates found, limiting its value as an up-to-date reference.
critical_path_items: 1) Availability of a reliable base EV vehicle to convert into the driverless mule - this was the actual, ultimate blocker, since the base EV itself failed scrutineering or dynamic events in 2019, 2022, and 2023. 2) COVID-19's cancellation of FSAE-A in both 2020 and 2021, removing two full competition cycles of real-world deadline pressure and validation opportunity right as the driverless subsystems were being developed. 3) The driverless effort's organizational status as a capstone/junior student project (explicitly described this way in the May 2020 newsletter) rather than a permanently resourced core team function, which made it easy to deprioritize once the base EV needed rescuing.

validation_strategy: Validation remained entirely at the simulation/bench level throughout the program's documented life: fssim (Gazebo) for perception/SLAM, recorded sensor logs for offline analysis, and Assetto Corsa for driver-training purposes. No evidence of the team progressing to on-vehicle static or dynamic testing was found.
rules_compliance_challenges: The program never reached driverless-specific rules compliance (no evidence of DT.3.2 EBS work, DT.2.2 actuator decoupling, or DT.4 shutdown-circuit integration for an autonomous system). Instructively, even the team's non-driverless, standard EV shutdown/safety circuit was a documented, named point of failure that kept the base car out of dynamic events in 2023 ('safety shutdown circuit problems') - suggesting foundational LV/safety-circuit competence was itself a struggle for this team during the relevant years.
tech_inspection_experience: The base EV failed to reach dynamic events in 2019 (combustion engine issues prevented that class from competing at all; the electric car did complete some events), 2022 (electrical issues), and 2023 (safety shutdown circuit problems). The first full pass of technical inspections since 2019 came only in 2024 - and this was for the standard EV, not any driverless entry, which never existed as a competition entry.
ebs_test_experience: N/A - no EBS was ever built.
documentation_burden: [uncertain, partial] The driverless capstone project was required to produce a 'feasibility and safety' final report for university faculty, due end of May 2020 - a university/faculty-level compliance requirement specific to this team's academic-capstone structure for driverless, not standard FSAE competition documentation (DSF/ASF etc.), which was never reached since no driverless competition entry occurred.
dv_event_results: None. MUR never entered a driverless/autonomous class or event at any competition in any year for which results were found (official results history covers 2012-2024, listing only Combustion and Electric class results).
perception_range_achieved: [uncertain] Not quantified in any available source; perception subsystem work stayed at the simulation/bench stage.
reliability_notes: The base (non-driverless) EV vehicle failed to start or complete dynamic events in 5 of 6 seasons from 2019-2024 (2019 combustion failure, 2020-2021 COVID cancellations count as non-events, 2022 electrical issues, 2023 shutdown-circuit issues); only 2024 saw any dynamic-event participation (Endurance only). No driverless-specific reliability data exists because no driverless vehicle was ever fielded at competition.
top_mistakes: Inferred from the documented pattern (no direct MUR quote on 'mistakes' was found, unlike EUFS's alumni post): (1) Running driverless as a capstone/junior side-project rather than a permanently resourced core program meant it had no protected budget or headcount when the base EV needed rescuing, and it was the first thing dropped. (2) Planning to inherit the team's own used competition EV as the driverless mule (MUR2021E -> MUR2022D) instead of securing a separate, dedicated or simplified test platform made driverless progress fully hostage to the main EV program's own reliability problems. (3) Spending roughly 2 years (2019-2021) in simulation/bench-only development without ever mounting any subsystem on a physical vehicle meant that team knowledge and momentum were never converted into hardware progress before COVID and the 2022 program reset hit. [uncertain - this is an inference from the documented timeline, not a quoted team retrospective]
advice_for_new_teams: [uncertain] No first-hand 'advice to new teams' statement from MUR itself was found (in contrast to EUFS, which has a detailed alumni how-to post). The strongest available signal is implicit, not quoted: MUR's own retrospective language ('started afresh focusing solely on building an EV car') indicates the team judged driverless as unaffordable alongside a struggling core EV program - i.e., their implicit lesson is that a reliable base vehicle must come before a driverless conversion attempt.
team_structure_dv: As of March 2020, the driverless effort was organized into two subsystems: 'Perception and spatial' and 'Control and path planning' (per the team blog's first 'About' post). It was run substantially as a capstone project for final-year students, supplemented by junior projects (continuous integration server, human collision avoidance, a 3D-printed car) per the May 2020 newsletter. No specific headcount figures were found for the driverless sub-team at any point. By 2022 there is no evidence the driverless sub-team still existed as a distinct, staffed group.
recruiting_and_knowledge_transfer: The public engineering blog (murdriverless.github.io, ~17 posts Mar-Sep 2020, one further post Jul 2021) functioned as the team's primary documented knowledge-transfer mechanism. It stopped updating after July 2021, coinciding with the program's apparent discontinuation - suggesting knowledge transfer collapsed alongside the broader program lapse, illustrating a common single-point-of-failure risk when a driverless effort is a side project rather than embedded in core team process and succession planning.
budget_estimate: [uncertain] Not disclosed in any source found, for either the driverless program specifically or MUR's whole-team budget.
recommended_sequence: Synthesized/inferred from what went wrong at MUR (not a quoted MUR recommendation): 1) Secure a reliable base vehicle FIRST and prove it can pass scrutineering and complete dynamic events before allocating engineering time to a driverless conversion. 2) Do not plan to convert the team's only/most-recent competition car into the driverless mule - use a separate, disposable, or simplified rig instead, so a base-EV setback cannot stall the driverless program. 3) Treat driverless as a resourced core program with protected headcount, not a capstone/junior side project whose people can be reassigned the moment the main car needs rescuing. 4) Get subsystems onto physical hardware early, even non-FS test rigs - MUR's own HuskyControl repository suggests an intent to test control algorithms on a Clearpath Husky ground robot before car integration, a sound instinct that does not appear to have been followed through to the actual car. 5) Maintain public/internal documentation continuously as a leading indicator of program health - MUR's blog stopping in mid-2021 mirrors the program's own stall almost exactly.
applicability_to_24_month_ramp: MUR's case functions as a cautionary counter-example, not a template, for a requester with a running EV, ~9 software-focused members, and a 24-month window: MUR had a comparable or larger resource base and, unlike the requester, an explicit plan to reuse an existing EV - yet still failed to reach a single autonomous run after 7+ years (2019-2026), primarily because (a) the base EV itself was not reliably competition-ready for 3 of those years (2019, 2022, 2023) and (b) driverless was never protected as its own program once the main vehicle needed rescuing. Direct, actionable takeaways for the requester: (1) since they already have a running EV (the precondition MUR never durably had), they should lock down and verify that vehicle's reliability/scrutineering-readiness BEFORE committing significant engineering time to the driverless conversion; (2) explicitly ring-fence the ~9 driverless engineers with protected scope so they are not reassigned to rescue the base car the way MUR's capstone team effectively was; (3) get every subsystem onto physical hardware (even a non-competition mule, not the team's only competition car) within the first 6-9 months rather than spending 18-24 months in simulation/bench-only development as MUR did; (4) treat continuous public/internal documentation and blog-style progress tracking as an early-warning system for program health, since MUR's own documentation trail stopping in mid-2021 was itself the clearest external signal that the program had stalled.
